# WalkCast.FM - thejaymo.net

I tried out a new App called [WalkCast](https://www.walkcast.fm/about) today developed by [oio studio](https://oio.studio/).

They bill it as a “Story Telling Engine,” which is definitely more snappy than saying it’s an: *AI powered – location based – narrative non fiction – podcast generator?*

It’s quite a fun little app. I’m reposting their marketing video below, as I can’t seem to link directly to it:

[![Screenshot of the Walk Cast web interface by oio, featuring colorful abstract gradient shapes. Text reads: WALK CAST, an ever-changing podcast generated on the spot by oio. Below a central play button, text says: this episode is sponsored by Vivi R, 71 episodes left. Navigation links at the bottom: what is it?, sponsor, terms.](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20516%201024'%3E%3C/svg%3E)![Screenshot of the Walk Cast web interface by oio, featuring colorful abstract gradient shapes. Text reads: WALK CAST, an ever-changing podcast generated on the spot by oio. Below a central play button, text says: this episode is sponsored by Vivi R, 71 episodes left. Navigation links at the bottom: what is it?, sponsor, terms.](https://thejaymo.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Screenshot-2024-10-15-at-11.21.24-516x1024-png.webp)](https://www.walkcast.fm/)

## How it Works

The app grabs your location, searches the web for information about where you are, generates a narrative text summary, and spits it out as audio. On the about page, they hint that there’s a lot more happening behind the scenes, but essentially that’s the experience.

> Imagine it as a series of intelligent agents—curator, editor, and
> host—each with a distinct role in the creation of every story. The
> curator digs deep into your surroundings, finding facts and points of
> interest. The editor weaves these into a dynamic script, sometimes
> adding creative tangents and surprising twists.
>
> Finally, the host—our AI-generated voice—delivers the story, always in
> the perfect tone. This loop continues as long as you keep walking,
> transforming every step into a suprising moment.
>
> In the end, here at [oio](https://oio.studio/) we’re
> on a mission to create products and tools for a less-boring future, and
> waiting for someone else to do it just wasn’t an option. So we built it
> ourselves.
>
> @oio.studio <https://www.walkcast.fm/about>

I recently made an episode of *301* about [Googles NotebookLM](https://thejaymo.net/2024/09/28/2425-notebookfm/) where I self inserted an AI version of my own voice into the ‘podcast’ it generated about my own work. I’ve also written about the [weird issues](https://thejaymo.net/2024/05/14/gpt-4o-must-die/) that we are going to have to [confront in the medium term](https://thejaymo.net/2024/09/10/virtual-a-friends-real-feelings/).

But never the less, personality driven front ends for AI systems are an emerging UX paradigm and and WalkCast fits right into that space and have made something quite compelling. But having tried it, I also have some problems with it.

## My Immediate Challanges

I went for a walk with the app this morning and experienced it twice (each session lasting about 7–10 minutes). The best way to describe it is that it felt like being ‘inside Wikipedia.’ The infosphere was narratively augmented over my direct physical environment.

For the first five minutes or so, it really does feel like a Location-Specific Experience. But as you continue to use the app, the narrative presentation about the place you’re in starts to feel flat.

One issue was the repetitive structure of the narratives. Each experience followed the same pattern: first, some facts about the immediate location, then a zoom-out to a broader area, followed by a tenuous metaphor. For example, I listened to a story about [Seething Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seething_Wells) that morphed into a spooky ghost tale, which then swerved into an NPR-style metaphor about jellyfish (yes, jellyfish!) and tunnels, before zooming out to [Surbiton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surbiton) and ending with another odd connection to fungi and arts and crafts. It was weirdly disjointed.

This brings up a bigger issue: **narrative nonfiction ≠ story.** A good story has structure, pacing, and a sense of direction, but WalkCast lacks that. There’s no feedback loop responding to the user’s actions or movement. Even museum audio guides provide more agency than this app by letting listeners control what they hear and when. I was expecting something more interactive—perhaps a ‘choose your own adventure’ vibe, where the app could suggest going left to learn about X or right to hear about Y.

## Spatial Storytelling

My friend Rob Morgan has a book coming out in December on CRC Press: *[Storytelling for Spatial Computing and Mixed Reality: The Art of Augmenting Imagination](https://www.routledge.com/Storytelling-for-Spatial-Computing-and-Mixed-Reality-The-Art-of-Augmenting-Imagination/Morgan/p/book/9781032459271?srsltid=AfmBOoqU3HXhRHmE8MRjcZxtZvVB5otEBFm2eXd9lpevOyf2lU7lEXzj)*. In the interests of full disclosure I have a blurb on the jacket:

> A vision for storytelling in the coming age of spatial computing. Offering a mix of practical guidance and speculative theory, Morgan equips readers for the narrative possibilities ahead. A primer and a gateway to next-gen storytelling in virtual worlds of all kinds.
>
> **Jay Springett – Researcher & Worldrunner**
>
>  <https://www.routledge.com/Storytelling-for-Spatial-Computing-and-Mixed-Reality-The-Art-of-Augmenting-Imagination/Morgan/p/book/9781032459271>

Rob began his career working in VR and more recently in location-based augmented reality theatre with his company [Playlines](https://playlines.net/). I’ve been very fortunate to have read several drafts of his book over the last year and as a result, can only really think of WalkCast though the lens of his work. Which is difficult as I want to quote so much from it as the book isn’t out yet!

Rob spends a great deal of the book discussing *AUGMENTING PLACES* (Section 4) and explaining the different design philosophies of *Augmented Location-Agnostic Experiences* and *Location-Specific Experiences* as well as another he calls ‘*location-portable*‘. Its all too much detail to go into but there are a couple of things that come to mind.

It’s tempting to say that WalkCast have made a *Location-Specific Experience*. After all you fire up the app and find yourself immersed in the infospehere of the place around you. Satisfying Gordon Calleja’s insistence that to create ‘immersion’ the techno-social system must *“acknowledgement of the player’s location and presence.*” (I’ve written about [Calleja’s work here](https://thejaymo.net/2023/10/15/301-2333-presence-in-worlds/)).

## Improvements

One of the key elements of augmented/spatial narrative design is that is that the audience is not just a witness to the narrative but are inside of it. WalkCast fails because there’s no story to be inside of, there’s no sequence of events, no sense making. It literally is just Wikipedia being pipped into your earholes.

A key insight that Rob is that when you are designing these sorts of experiences, there’s a tension between augmenting places and augmenting the player. And WalkCast should have a think about which paradigm they are working in what they have right now is a sort of location-portable / or site agnostic design. But there’s probably more value in remembering Rob’s second rule: ***the most important reality you are augmenting is the player themselves.***

The experience could be massively improved by ditching the weird metaphors editorial and instead just refetch the user’s location as they walk. In a dense city like London, almost every street has an interesting history or a Wikipedia page. Updating the narrative in real time as you walk would create a more engaging and immersive experience. WalkCast needs to decide if they want to lean into narrative nonfiction or develop true stories. AI powered Wikipedia for your ears is going to get old really quickly.

I do however see *huge* potential in WalkCast, its a really fun little demo/toy. I’m looking forward to seeing how it and similar apps evolve.

# Start Select Reset Zine - Return of the Real - thejaymo.net

Starting today, Start Select Reset Zine will be sent via sail mail to paid supporters subscribed at £5 a Month or above 4 times a year. [Sign up to get issue #002.](https://thejaymo.net/support/)

[![A folded white zine with START SELECT RESET in bold text and #002 handwritten, resting on colorful papers beside blurred green plant leaves.](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%202204%201240'%3E%3C/svg%3E)![A folded white zine with START SELECT RESET in bold text and #002 handwritten, resting on colorful papers beside blurred green plant leaves.](https://thejaymo.net/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/PXL_20220429_140725135.PORTRAIT_2-edited-jpg.webp)](https://thejaymo.net/support/)

[SSR 002](https://thejaymo.net/support/)

SSRZ #002 – Return of the Real is 1 sheet of double sided A4 laser printed on 120 gsm colour paper, hand folded and posted by me.

### [Show Supporter 📻](https://buy.stripe.com/00g16oe2T1Nd6FW288)

***Support the Show***  
[Quarterly zine](https://thejaymo.net/zine/); my gift to you.

[£5 Monthly 👏](https://buy.stripe.com/00g16oe2T1Nd6FW288)

Cancel any time. Delivery is quarterly.

### [Yearly Patron 🏆](https://buy.stripe.com/bIY6qI6Ar77xe8ofYZ)

Same zine; bigger backing.  
Yearly support, quarterly mail.

[£100 Yearly 📆](https://buy.stripe.com/bIY6qI6Ar77xe8ofYZ)

Cancel any time.

*International zines are posted with full customs declarations as printed booklets. Local VAT, customs, or handling fees may be due on arrival.*

[![A fan of colorful folded zines on a wooden table, each printed with bold black START SELECT RESET text and the handwritten number #002.](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201024%20576'%3E%3C/svg%3E)![A fan of colorful folded zines on a wooden table, each printed with bold black START SELECT RESET text and the handwritten number #002.](https://thejaymo.net/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/PXL_20220503_153728005-1024x576.jpeg)](https://thejaymo.net/support/)

[SSR 002](https://thejaymo.net/support/)

---

## Why Start A Physical Newsletter in 2022?

In September of 2018 I put out a collection of [podcast transcripts](https://thejaymo.net/permanentlymoved/) on the attention economy and social media as PDF called [Start Select Reset Zine #001 – Your Attention Is Sovereign](https://content.libsyn.com/p/0/5/7/0573858d24462354/SSRZ_-_001_-_Your_Attention_Is_Sovereign.pdf?c_id=51790010&cs_id=51790010&response-content-type=application%2Fpdf&Expires=1651665823&Signature=B9y5Qk5LiCO7RLXBqnodKc54UjDh6gT3ZgyHlw8AYQSQvnor-ngG4Cmwr6Qpk3Jjfip4Xs8xCuJLX28mRHIS0qvKBOscHMjCZUgwkvZ2gIPsh2wCouMbTH6iSiWIB11-M5gbeEMaViJopX92T1SUI80lWyl-wv6b2WgXzyR-l5~U3P7aSBhvox0mTnwJ~6fVVDm3821JTZoPcsBnjXsL43d9ApjE8dJUG7FdC0f0fLuo1AHluiC1oE26bPGCV1jrJos06Q4KYeCdTfvvdxsPjgFGfXGEHXyLFTgqBB~cP3-fCs4e1cpJ1HkzoFa8QBPGMjrQOsDvd8R5PdMyPsbL-A__&Key-Pair-Id=K1YS7LZGUP96OI). Since then it has been download over 14,000 times.

Back then my intention was to continue to collect podcast transcripts and post them as PDF zines online. But creator friends encouraged me to post [Permanently Moved](https://permanentlymoved.online/) episode transcripts as as blog posts online instead. Both for accessibility reasons and my own reference – this proved to be correct advice.

In 2020, I launched the [paid supporter](https://thejaymo.net/support/) page on my site. At the time I didn’t want to put 301 behind a paywall in anyway shape or form. Instead asking people to support the show if they liked it – I am extremely grateful to all those who have subscribed and supported my work so far.

Going in to 2022 I hadn’t made any more zines but really wanted to. I also continue to make the show and post it on the internet for free.

One of the problems I have been experiencing however is the dreaded *‘value proposition’.* What do paid supporters get in return for their support? Until today the answer has been nothing. From today:

Paid supporters Subscribed at £5 a Month or £100 a Year will receive a hand made zine via snail mail seasonally.

Making 301 every week, writing the essay, recording, editing the video and audio versions is in all honestly, a huge amount of work. I’ve set the value on these zines 4 times a year at a level that I think is fair and comparable to other types of value supplied by creators substacks and patreons that I pay for myself. I mean this sure sounds (to me) like better value than paying 5 bucks a month in exchange for emails?

As I was moaning about [the other week](https://thejaymo.net/2022/04/24/242-double-down/), I still need to set up the infrastructure to better support the subscription levels, people’s address’s and zine shipping. But all this costs money. I’m hoping that any new subscribers will boot strap the funds to sort this out.

For now, if you subscribe you will receive an email from me asking for your address.

Once the zines are gone, they are gone – if any remain when the next issue goes out in August, they will go up for sale on thejaymo.net.

[![A white folded zine titled START SELECT RESET #002, surrounded by similar orange, green, and blue booklets on a wooden surface.](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201024%20771'%3E%3C/svg%3E)![A white folded zine titled START SELECT RESET #002, surrounded by similar orange, green, and blue booklets on a wooden surface.](https://thejaymo.net/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/PXL_20220503_153754498.PORTRAIT-1024x771.jpg)](https://thejaymo.net/support/)

[SSR 002](https://thejaymo.net/support/)

---

My friend JD O – [Check out his 301 podcast episode](https://thejaymo.net/2021/06/12/301-2123-jdo-the-dark-souls-method/) – recently withdrew ‘pay what you want’ pricing for his novels and set fixed price on Gumroad instead. Like me, JD O is a child of the 90’s, Napster, Soulseek etc – influenced by the early ‘Information Wants to Be Free’ web.

But in 2022 this is unsustainable. Here’s what JD O wrote about why he was re-pricing his novels

> the act of writing and reading are *sacred*, meaning they require *sacrifice* to fully appreciate/realize/experience.
>
> You pay a Tarot reader before a reading. You have to. Same with any magical exchange. Don’t go asking spirits for things unless you’re ready to leave an orange and some incense at the very least. And the same holds true of the “ritual space” of art experience. Reading a book, watching a movie, listening to music, playing a video game, admiring a painting…all of it requires payment, especially if it affects you.
>
> Payment can be monetary, or perhaps spreading a little “word of mouth,” but in 2022, it’s monetary. It *feels* good, feels right, to pay for things you enjoy. And then you can share them!
>
>  <https://brokenriverbooks.com/2022/05/03/paying-for-art-05-03-22/>

In 2019 I wrote *the only reason you’re not selling out is because nobody is buying.* Lots of people thanked me for that line at the time, but I didn’t take my own advice. People had nothing to buy that they couldn’t already get for free.

I’m starting a physical zine, a physical newsletter, in 2022 because I belive thats where I belive *real value* is.

As our culture moves / trends towards ever greater levels of abstraction, making and sending *real things* to *real people* is the way forward. The essay in issue #002 is all about this ‘real’.

If you become a paid supporter, you are *paying for* the zine/newsletter and getting my weekly podcast *for free*.

I hope you will consider supporting me.

## [Support my Work 💪](https://thejaymo.net/support/)

*Keep things up and running.*

[£5 Monthly 👏](https://buy.stripe.com/00g16oe2T1Nd6FW288)

*[Includes handmade zine](https://thejaymo.net/zine/).*

source_markdown:
# Using personal weeknotes as a tool for attention

Since leaving my day job two years ago, I’ve been writing [personal weeknotes](https://tracydurnell.com/category/weeknotes/). In short: once a week, I publish on my blog a set of notes about what I did the past week. I believe weeknotes started inside organizations, but **I appreciate using the weekly checkpoint as a personal tool to steer my attention and action**.

*This post is my entry for July’s [IndieWeb Carnival](https://indieweb.org/indieweb-carnival) [on the theme of tools](https://jamesg.blog/2024/07/01/indieweb-carnival-tools/), hosted by James G. [Crossposted to IndieNews](https://news.indieweb.org/en).*

## Why I started keeping personal weeknotes

I knew, as I was transitioning from an externally-structured schedule to a [self-defined one](https://tracydurnell.com/2023/03/18/swimming-outside-the-lanes/), that I would be [susceptible to feelings](https://tracydurnell.com/2022/02/22/the-reckoning-of-the-to-do-list/) of [not doing enough](https://tracydurnell.com/2023/02/20/the-work-is-not-enough/). It’s easy for me to trip over issues of self-worth related to work and worries about carrying my fair share in my partnership. (Fortunately, my partner has been my biggest cheerleader for both betting on myself and acknowledging that we don’t need to “pencil out” our contributions to be equal partners.) As I started my journey of self-employment, I needed to [balance](https://tracydurnell.com/2022/09/14/rest-ethic/) those fears of [not doing enough](https://tracydurnell.com/2023/10/08/accepting-the-capacity-gap/) with [my state of burnout and exhaustion](https://tracydurnell.com/2023/05/24/assuming-no-change-is-an-option/), taking time to rest while also making progress.

I noticed other bloggers writing weeknotes, both professional and personal. At first, I was simply interested in the contents of what people were doing — and then I recognized the usefulness of weeknotes as a tool.

### Weeknotes are a multipurpose tool

Weeknotes are a **tool for awareness**, helping me learn what I’m capable of doing in a week so I can make reasonable plans for the future — both for work and life. They also serve as a record of what I \*did\* do, reminding me of things that I might have forgotten.

Weeknotes let me **externalize my internal goals**. I’ve had trouble sticking to goals I’ve set for myself in the past, with external accountability being a much more powerful driver. They provide **gentle accountability** through publishing them publicly. Committing to publishing gives me a specific time to do them and helps me follow through on actually completing the weeknotes. Some of the things I track are both useful to me *and*  a way to participate in [indie web discovery](https://tracydurnell.com/2024/05/24/indie-web-curation-and-collation/), which gives me another nudge.

Weeknotes are a means to **shape my own behavior**. **Headings serve as prompts**: knowing I have a slot in the template waiting for me to fill in on Fridays is a reminder — and motivation — for me to do things that I value but might not make time for (like listen to new music). **Because I design my own format, weeknotes reinforce *my* priorities.**

### What I like about personal weeknotes as a tool

I’m good about starting the week off with a to-do list, but I had trouble getting any end-of-week process to stick. Weeknotes are what’s finally worked for me. It’s become a **marking point for me to divide time** since I work from home, so weeks and months can easily blur together since I lack physical cues.

I’ve experimented with a variety of accountability methods, including monthly and quarterly check-ins, but **the weekly cadence influences my behavior whereas longer time periods become retrospective documentation**. For me, the once-a-week rhythm is what makes weeknotes a *tool* versus merely a record.

I have a tendency to get locked into formats prematurely, but treating weeknotes as a tool gives me the mental wiggle room to **change the format as suits me**.

## Creating my personal weeknote template

### First version: life categories

[For the first three months](https://cascadiainspired.com/week-notes-sabbatical-week-1/), I made notes organized by a set of life categories: creative work, career, play, learning, household, and health.

I’d chosen these “buckets” through my [personal annual review process](https://cascadiainspired.com/category/annual-review/), and used them for quarterly check-ins to make sure I stayed on track through the year. For weeknotes, though, I found them **too vague**, which meant that I tracked either too much or too little. At a quarterly scale, it was easier to identify what was “worth” keeping track of, but on a weekly basis, there were things I did that didn’t fit nicely into one category or another, and things I wanted to “give myself credit for” that didn’t seem big enough. The “demands” of each life category cycle at a different pace, too, not necessarily aligned with weeks.

By the time my post-quitting “sabbatical” ended, I recognized that format wasn’t what I needed.

### Version two: specific actions

I [restarted weeknotes](https://tracydurnell.com/2022/12/09/weeknotes-dec-3-9/) here in a different format. I can’t recall who I borrowed inspiration for the format from, but I started with:

- stuff I did
- what I read
- changes to my website

Since then, I’ve added more headings:

- words I looked up and concepts I learned
- pretty things I saw
- what I ate for dinner
- new music I listened to
- nature notes
- win of the week
- looking forward to

**Being specific makes the tool easy to use** — I don’t have to debate whether something belongs.

Some headings — new music, website changes, nature notes, words — might not have something every week, but I keep them in the template as a prompt. I tried out a few other headings that didn’t stick, and have a few floating headings that aren’t in the template but I’ll add on if it comes up.

## Why I log what I log

### Setting reasonable expectations

I wanted to track “stuff I did” to help myself **recognize how much happens in a week and set healthier self expectations**. My two actual “metrics” are how many hours I spent on paid consulting work (or sometimes business development) and how many hours I spent writing fiction. Everything else just gets a bullet point.

**I don’t track anything that could make me feel *actually* bad about myself.** I might be a little embarrassed if I don’t write as much as I wanted to, but no one’s going to judge me as a person for it — creative folks get it. The intention of my weeknotes [is not to shame myself](https://tracydurnell.com/2024/07/14/self-care-thats-not-driven-by-shame/).

### All my reading, not just what I finished

[I care about how much I read](https://tracydurnell.com/2023/08/19/my-reading-philosophy-and-17-reading-guidelines/), both because it signifies that I’ve made time for leisure and because I’m a fiction writer so reading stories supports storycraft. While I still log reads on Goodreads, I consider my website the canonical record of my reading. In my weeknotes, I track what I finished reading as well as what I spent time reading, what I quit reading, and any books I bought. Having each week’s reading in a condensed bullet point format means I notice right away if I haven’t been reading enough.

Originally, I also listed what I added to my to-read list, but that became annoying to cross-reference from Goodreads — and it made me feel a little guilty about [adding so many things to my TBR](https://tracydurnell.com/2023/11/02/appreciating-books-i-havent-read-yet/), which isn’t what I intended. **The nice thing about tools you make for yourself is that you get to change them when they don’t work the way you thought.**

### Pinpointing definitions

After reading *Several Short Sentences About Writing* and [*On Tyranny*](https://tracydurnell.com/2022/06/09/read-on-tyranny-graphic-edition/), I wanted to pay closer attention to [the specific meanings of words](https://tracydurnell.com/2023/03/25/the-tactic-of-destroying-the-meaning-of-words/), especially [which words and phrases I use in my own writing](https://tracydurnell.com/2022/12/28/meaning-through-truthfulness-in-language/).

Having a place to log the words and concepts I learn makes me **engage more closely with what I’m reading**. I notice more often when I’ve gleaned the meaning of a word from context, but don’t *really* know what it means. Sometimes I’ll try to define a word out loud to my husband (sorry babe), which typically makes undeniable the fact that I don’t know what I’m talking about 😂

**The way I compile my weeknotes reinforces the goal** to learn definitions more precisely. I add words to a draft post throughout the week, but I intentionally don’t link the definitions when I add them. That means I need to look up each word again at the end of the week to add the link. Before I look it up, I try to remember the definition — usually I’m wrong, so being forced to look at it a second time helps me learn it better.

(As I’ve been tracking [new-to-me words](https://tracydurnell.com/resources/words/), I have come to notice just how many are [bullshit](https://tracydurnell.com/2024/02/13/the-many-tongues-of-english/). Writers adjectivize or adverbify complex terms that I can barely understand on their own, let alone adapted into a modifier. (I *beg* you not to use the term synechdochical. I have looked it up So Many Times and I still don’t get it 🤦‍♀️😂) I am on board with the concept of words having a cost — and that a writer only has budget for a few $5 words per post or essay. Wanting to sound erudite (there goes my budget) leads us to [over-complicate the language we use](https://tracydurnell.com/2023/02/13/everyone-prefers-plain-language/). We should probably skip the $10 word, and the $25 word is just showing off.)

### A record of dinners

Choosing what to eat for dinner is the most contentious issue in my household because neither of us wants to decide 😂 I hoped that tracking what we ate would provide inspiration for future meals — it hasn’t happened thus far but that’s not to say it won’t 😉 The log does serve as a **handy reference**, though, since I link to any new recipes I make. I also look back when I can’t remember how old leftovers are 😄

### Participating in the indie web

While Instagram and Pinterest are guaranteed sources for visual inspiration, [I hate the world of infinite scroll](https://tracydurnell.com/2023/07/31/read-stolen-focus/). Giving myself a place to curate pretty things I’ve seen on the broader indie web **supports the indie mode of discovery** for anyone reading, and also **makes it easier for me** to celebrate cool things without making a dedicated post about it. It **encourages me to delve\* deeper** into an artist’s portfolio and explore their other work on their website.

\*(I hear ‘delve’ is a genAI indicator now but it’s too good a word to give up 😜 You can’t have it, learning machines!)

### Discovering new music without a streaming subscription

Cancelling my music streaming service [disrupted the system I used to discover new music](https://tracydurnell.com/2023/04/25/listening-to-music-without-a-streaming-subscription/) over the previous decade. I [value listening to new music](https://tracydurnell.com/2022/08/19/new-music/), so this heading reminds me to make the effort.

It takes [more intentionality](https://tracydurnell.com/2024/05/09/taste-requires-intentional-attention/) to re-listen to songs without a streaming service, since there isn’t one place where all the new music I’ve tried lives; having a record lets me go back if I want to listen to a specific song again instead of being lost to the ether.

Even though I post all the new music I listen to the entire track, so it’s not precisely an endorsement, I still think it [**contributes to indie web discovery**](https://tracydurnell.com/2021/11/11/breaking-out-of-what-the-algorithm-feeds-you/). Having access to — and choosing from — the world’s entire pool of music is overwhelming, which is why discovery on streaming services happens [via algorithm](https://tracydurnell.com/2023/11/07/in-algorithm-we-trust/). A smaller set of options to sample from is way more human-friendly. I appreciate when other bloggers suggest music to try, so this is another **pay-it-forward category**.

### Watching my wildlife garden

I turned my yard into a wildlife garden, and now I see animals all the time 😃🥰 Having this section reminds me to pay attention to what’s happening outside in my yard — I’ve identified more birds in the past couple months than previous years 😲 ([Moving the birdbath](https://cascadiainspired.com/imperfection-through-gardening/) in front of the kitchen window helped too.) These are birds that \*live in my backyard\* so I could have been spotting them all along 😅 It’s **a prompt to immerse myself in my physical space**: to notice what’s changed, and to appreciate the results of all my and my husband’s hard work.

I also think the science of ecological timing — [phenology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phenology) — is extremely cool and [important in a world of climate change](https://tracydurnell.com/2022/10/17/climate-change-makes-animal-populations-more-susceptible-to-other-impacts/). It’s also [an easy thing for hobbyists to track](https://tracydurnell.com/2024/02/19/things-to-do-with-a-website/). I only added this heading this spring, so I’m looking forward to building up more than a year’s log so I can compare timing between years!

### Choosing highlights

I pick a win for the week and identify something I’m looking forward to. This is **a practice in positivity** that forces me to reflect on the week, specifically looking for the good stuff rather than dwelling on the bad. It’s also a **reminder** to plan things to look forward to. These prompts are both challenging for me, so they’re usually the last thing I complete in my weeknotes each week 😉

## Some other people’s weeknotes I enjoy

It seems like a good number of bloggers are writing weeknotes these days! Here are a few that I enjoy:

- Alice Bartlett’s weeknotes are often hilarious even as I am sympathetic to the b.s.! — [most recent](https://alicebartlett.co.uk/blog/weaknotes-308)
- Anh publishes periodic weeknotes that have a bit different format each time, which is fun — [most recent](https://anhvn.com/posts/2024/weeknotes-17/)
- Jay Springett rounds up creative work from the week as well as some commentary and recommendations — I am taken with the phrase “ministry of my own labour” — [most recent](https://www.thejaymo.net/2024/07/28/349-birthday-39/)

Because I design my own format, weeknotes reinforce my priorities.

source_markdown:
### **Taking an Internet Walk** ##### *by* *[Spencer Chang](https://syllabusproject.org/spencer-chang/) & [Kristoffer Tjalve](https://syllabusproject.org/kristoffer-tjalve/)* ##### **THE INTERNET AS WE KNOW IT** In futuristic and cyberpunk media, we were promised a technological world “indistinguishable from magic:” from flying cars to perpetual motion machines to computers inside our heads. The drive of these future-pointing imaginations is to make the things we already have more powerful, less annoying, and most of all, ubiquitous. In the present, we have the Internet. What was once described as “[an alien life form](https://www.unilad.com/technology/david-bowie-predicts-internet-1999-20221018#:~:text=%22No%20it%27s%20not.%20No%2C%20it%27s%20an%20alien%20life%20form.%22),” has now become mundane. It is only natural, we think, that the only thing we have in common with those we share the train with is that we are all, neck craned down, staring at our phones. It is the way the world works, we think, that our “internet” comprises the same 10 apps, some flooded with ads and spyware, others with people yelling about everything and nothing. We accept that the only way to get anything useful out of the internet is by trading our privacy for accounts and our self-expression for conformity. Everything is always somehow broken and when [social spaces die](https://kylechayka.substack.com/p/grief-for-twitter?publication_id=4425&post_id=137845749&isFreemail=true&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjozMzYzNDA2LCJwb3N0X2lkIjoxMzc4NDU3NDksImlhdCI6MTY5NzAzMjg1OSwiZXhwIjoxNjk5NjI0ODU5LCJpc3MiOiJwdWItNDQyNSIsInN1YiI6InBvc3QtcmVhY3Rpb24ifQ.U-i4P6-lohNq9zV-8YqqlVJOMYyBHwrW2Iz9KXkOAYw&r=2037y), we believe that it is how it has always been and that nothing will ever be different. We are here to take you by the hand and show you another Internet than the one sketched above. The Internet is so much vaster than a single worldview. It is a sprawling galaxy of archipelagos, filled with more humanity and personal gestures than any man-made archive. Instead of traversing the congested highways of the web, we invite you to try alternative routes: take a scroll down local streets and wandering paths, try out someone else’s commute, rediscover the favorites of your neighborhood, and gather the friends you love in your favorite spots, quiet and comforting. Beneath social media and app hedges, the blossoming internet awaits: a live ecosystem unfolding beneath our footsteps. ##### **1. ALTERNATIVE PATH SYSTEMS** In the 1950-70s, urban highways were built across many cities. It is beyond our syllabus to reason why parks, lakes, and sidewalks were sacrificed for additional car lanes,[1](https://syllabusproject.org/syllabus-for-taking-an-internet-walk/#897a0ef4-041d-4868-a860-1ee739262163) but, as these high-speed traffic veins warped the faces of neighborhoods, so have the introduction of search engines and social news feeds changed our online behavior. Fortunately, on the Internet, we still have the agency to wayfind through alternative path systems. ![An image of a man surfing down a slightly flooded urban street, a bus and palm trees in the background. ](https://i0.wp.com/syllabusproject.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/image4.png?resize=564%2C397&ssl=1) *[Image source](https://www.google.com/url?q=https://archives.starbulletin.com/2007/05/26/features/wood.html&sa=D&source=docs&ust=1699391549006025&usg=AOvVaw12J0PeIbzbvJNGqySJT3JG)* - Google “Alternative search engines.” There are many. Two of our favorites are [Wiby.me](https://wiby.me/) and [Metaphor.systems](https://metaphor.systems/). - If you are looking for a Sunday ride, we recommend visiting [River](https://river.maxbittker.com/) to traverse visually. Remember to turn on sounds and right-click to open in Are.na. - Make an [Are.na](https://www.are.na/) account, navigate to the [explore page](https://www.are.na/explore), filter to only images, click on the first thing catching your attention and explore the channel it belongs to. - Use the site-specific search on Google by using “site:reddit.com” or “site:webcurios.co.uk” to narrow in on specific communities. - Use Google reverse image search find the source of an image and exact keyword search (e.g. “cyberfeminism”). ##### **2. HYPERLINKS: FROM BLUE TO PURPLE** The first hyperlinks pointed within their own domain, like the doors separating the rooms in your home. However, with the world wide web, the doors became portals, and pioneers mapped out site directories to guide internet travelers to the frontier of development. Reject modern interstates and embody Tarzan, Jane, or the chimpanzee to swing from link to link, blue to purple. ![Disney's Cinderella walks down a staircase made up of tons and tons of windows cascading on top of one another. ](https://i0.wp.com/syllabusproject.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/image5.png?resize=1999%2C1125&ssl=1) *[Image source](https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.are.na/block/6921578&sa=D&source=docs&ust=1699391549004781&usg=AOvVaw18dnbTfuc-B8Fgm6635Ziy)* - Find a trailhead at a handmade index or collection. For example, if you like handmade websites, you should visit [Gossips Web](https://gossipsweb.net/) or [Brutalist Websites](https://brutalistwebsites.com/). These are the digital equivalent to the jazz bar, punk record store, or other physical places where subcultures gather. There’s likely one made by a devotee whatever your interest, like [cyberfeminism](https://cyberfeminismindex.com/), [tiny internet sites](https://www.are.na/spencer-chang/tiny-internets), [cozy websites](https://kristoffer.substack.com/), [niche museums](https://www.niche-museums.com/), [list of lists](https://arbesman.net/listoflists/), [LA sandwiches](https://krmr.com/sandwiches/), and [much more](https://sander.are.na/spencer-chang/collections-personal-documentation-archival). - Start your journey at [Everest Pipkin’s homepage](https://everest-pipkin.com/), it contains two webrings in the bottom-right. Webrings feel like visiting the friends of friends of friends. You’ll usually spot them at the bottom of a website. - Find a Wikipedia article for a word or subject that’s lingering with you and traverse the links that catch your eye (or use [The Wiki Game](https://www.thewikigame.com/group) to find a fun starting point). ##### **3. LOCAL COMMUNITY & NEIGHBORHOODS** Think of your favorite local spots near where you live. Everything from cozy cafes to welcoming libraries to the neighborhood specialty store. These are not the places that go viral on social media and get flooded by food-delivery pick-ups. They feel like *your* spots. You’re a regular there and learn the latest news from the community from the bulletin board. While you’re there, you run into your neighbors and hear about what they’ve been excited about. You’re able to offer support or ask for help when you need it. These local gathering spots and watering holes provide us the space for understanding who we are in community and give us a glimpse of solidarity. ![Text of an interview:

DAVID BRANCACCIO: There's a little sweet moment, I've got to say, in a very intense book--your latest--in which you're heading out the door and your wife says what are you doing? I think you say--I'm getting--I'm going to buy an envelope.

KURT VONNEGUT: Yeah.

DB: What happens then?

KV: Oh, she says well, you're not a poor man. You know, why don't you go online and buy a hundred envelopes and put them in the closet? And so I pretend not to hear her. And go out to get an envelope because I'm going to have a hell of a good time in the process of buying one envelope.

I meet a lot of people. And, see some great looking babes. And a fire engine goes by. And I give them the thumbs up. And, and ask a woman what kind of dog that is. And, and I don't know. The moral of the story is, is we're her on Earth to fart around.

And, of course, the computers will do us out of that. And, what hte computer people don't realize, or they don't care, is we're dancing animals. You know, we love to move around. And, we're not supposed to dance at all anymore. ](https://i0.wp.com/syllabusproject.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/image7.png?resize=523%2C264&ssl=1) *Kurt Vonnegut speaks of the magic of going out to buy an envelope. While our default experience of the internet feels more like what Kurt speaks of when he talks of computers, we believe that walking on the internet has this same magic (*[*source*](https://twitter.com/sfiegerman/status/805816421569753088)*).* - Instead of cranes and excavators, try to search for hands and wheelbarrows. Good places to start are [Neocities](https://neocities.org/browse), [mmm.page](https://build.mmm.page/explore), [Sheet Sites](https://ambient.institute/i/sheets/), [Your World of Text](https://www.yourworldoftext.com/) and [Tilde.club](https://tilde.club/users/). - Visit tiny social networks: cozy discords, [niche forums](https://forum.merveilles.town/), [online radio](https://www.are.na/alejandro-a/online-radios-39n-v3zqkvg), hyper-specific subreddits, local [chatrooms](https://volvox.observer/pond), [pubs](https://midnight.pub/), and [fields](https://cloudwatching.glitch.me/clouds). - Explore your [local artisans](https://sander.are.na/spencer-chang/small-tools-a4cx3duticc) when you need to accomplish a specific task: whether finding [new words](https://carefulwords.com/), picking [colors](https://meodai.github.io/poline/), or creating [pretty script](https://lingojam.com/ItalicTextGenerator). - Explore sites with their own environments and leave them in the corner of your computer, like [windows from around the world](https://www.window-swap.com/), [nesting eagles](http://sfbayospreys.org/), and [shifting gardens](https://htmlgarden.spencerchang.me/). ##### **4. FRIENDS OF FRIENDS** “I’m going to Athens, what should I do?” is a question we encounter in many variations. It’s not because the internet is not vast with recommendations, but discovering new places is also a social (and identity-forming) activity: we care about sharing tips with friends, knowing that they too, will sit on the bench in the National Garden, below the palm and in front of the purling creek, where we first read Deborah Levy’s *Real Estate*. ![A field of black arrow cursors are scattered over an image of a blue sky above a green-ish yellow cloud. ](https://i0.wp.com/syllabusproject.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/image6.png?resize=1999%2C1124&ssl=1) *[Image source](https://www.google.com/url?q=https://garden3d.substack.com/p/substantive-sustainability-gets-more&sa=D&source=docs&ust=1699391549133980&usg=AOvVaw3tp7GBDI4t_hyDAD5zU5__)* - Hand your phone to your friends, and let them scroll through your Instagram feed. This activity works particularly well if you are in a new location, or in a new group of friends. - In an incognito browser window, go to YouTube. Try to follow a particular niche by watching videos from the suggestions to the right. Alternatively, take a shortcut by exploring the filters of [Their Tube](https://www.their.tube/). - Join a [Screenwalks.com](https://screenwalks.com/) event, browse the archive of [Come Internet With Me](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLpGDRBad3EgWZyufVCOg8f_EKR8mDgQ14), or host your own screen-sharing session where you invite friends and strangers to watch your internet walks. ##### **5. FORAGING BEHIND THE SCENES** As kids, we counted the rings of a tree to discover its age. It felt like reading a secret message, similar to those we wrote with lemon juice. On the web, we don’t need to cut down a tree to count its age or heat the paper to reveal the message, because we can view the source of any page, telling us how it is made or poetic reflections. Take an excursion behind the scenes. ![A man in a big control room with carts containing big computers and other electronic machines with knobs, fiddles with the knob on a television that displays a rainbow of stripes. ](https://i0.wp.com/syllabusproject.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/image8.png?resize=1200%2C900&ssl=1) *Walter Bruch, PAL Television. [Image source](https://www.google.com/url?q=https://d2w9rnfcy7mm78.cloudfront.net/10751193/original_3dffc1264772ce53cb3689ffb3026117.png?1613338771?bc%3D0&sa=D&source=docs&ust=1699391548990011&usg=AOvVaw3Ycs8LV_0-3uXmjlXWWSv6).* - Right-click a page and click “Inspect Source”. Check for example [Taper](https://taper.badquar.to/), an online literary magazine where the artists’ statements are written in the source code. - Visit [Alt-Text as Poetry](https://alt-text-as-poetry.net/), to see the text descriptions the creators left. - Look for an open-source link on the website to see the messages left behind by the creator in their [commit log](https://github.com/spencerc99/spencerc99.github.io/commits/main). - Download [wwwwords](https://wwwwords.de/) to read about web accessibility. ##### **6. FIELD POCKET COMPUTER** Most of us walk with the internet every day, through the internet computer in our pockets. We know how to use it to listen to music louder than our surroundings, get traffic updates and navigational advice, and keep up with the latest news from around the world. But if you find yourself craving a more balanced experience, the field computer can help interweave the internet with your physical environment, the facilitator of an IRL Internet walk. - Make your own [“touch grass” focus mode](https://twitter.com/spencerc99/status/1710067598635708524) for a distraction-free phone mode[2](https://syllabusproject.org/syllabus-for-taking-an-internet-walk/#a7199412-f87a-40fe-ac70-313cf45ecc27) - Practice [dérive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%A9rive) by following some [wandering prompts](https://wanderprompts.com/) - Discover [queer experiences and share your own](https://www.queeringthemap.com/) - Explore your [city’s trees](https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2022/san-francisco-street-trees/) - Observe how the [shade on a block](https://shademap.app/@37.9842,23.7353,15z,1698651791753t,0b,0p,0m) will change as the sun rises or sets - Learn local [fauna](https://merlin.allaboutbirds.org/), [flora](https://myplantum.com/) and [histories](https://wiki-map.com/map) ##### **7. THE THINGS WE CARRY & KEEP** The bag has become an indispensable accessory to the modern urban dweller. As we travel through the city between our plans, our bags carry everything we need for our day out. Perhaps we designate certain bags as our “cafe bag,” the “working satchel,” or our “pochade box.” On the internet, our bags are as big as Mary Poppins’. We can stuff everything interesting we find into them, gathering snippets of [found text](https://particularly.online/), wayside images, and buried links to [collage](https://syllabusproject.org/on-the-world-as-collage-or-intertextuality/#nguyen2) them into messy worlds. The act of archiving is beyond preservation and extending memory; it shapes how we perceive and engage with the world. [Ursula Le Guin writes](https://otherfutures.nl/uploads/documents/le-guin-the-carrier-bag-theory-of-fiction.pdf) that the power of the carrier bag is the power of fiction, through our gatherings, we create worlds of our perspective. In our digital foraging and subsequent organizing, we create containers for [who we are](https://www.nylon.com/fashion/whats-in-my-bag-culture-and-putting-identity-on-display) and what we find important. [![A woman sits in front of a desktop background that contains an image of a river and trees, and is filled with files, apps, and shortcuts. ](https://i0.wp.com/syllabusproject.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/image3.png?resize=1999%2C1041&ssl=1)](https://mollysoda.exposed/) *[Molly Soda](https://mollysoda.exposed/)* - Record ordinary moments in [themed journals](https://www.writing.upenn.edu/library/Mayer-Bernadette_Experiments.html). - Keep a running list of [all the moments you’ve been appreciated](https://twitter.com/j_asminewang/status/1430009013983350807) or the times you’ve been [overwhelmed with gratitude for life](https://spencers.cafe/projects/i-love-living), save these as [emotional Tupperware](https://ansonyu.me/tupperware) for a tough day - Cherish the history embedded in your unclosed browser tabs. - Gather things you love in folk databases: [spreadsheets](https://www.are.na/megan-dieudonne/useful-and-good-google-docs-and-sheets), bulleted lists, and [slideshows](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1GWSFltGp0Qr9YKzu4cc_4eGhFcWCrzGN0zn5G0vp3mE/edit#slide=id.g1022b30457c_0_15) and open link access to the public. - Revisit the “links” section in conversations with your favorite people to revisit an archive of what has made you think of each other. - Use your phone to record audio of places that make your heart sing. Replay the clips when you find your mind caught up in the flurry of the everyday. - Maintain a “photo of the day” album to collect scenes from your life. You can also use the “favorite” photo functionality for this as a convenient alternative. - Try [Glance Back](https://glanceback.info/), an extension that takes a photo of you using the computer at a random time every day. Consider these your computer portraits and use the caption feature to write what website you were about to visit. - Make a [Screenshot Garden](https://screenshot-garden.neocities.org/build-your-own) to collect all your digital trash and treasures. These become the material for your digital collages. If this sounds foreign to you, visit [Molly Soda](https://mollysoda.exposed/)’s website. - Create containers for different discoveries. For example, Laurel Schwulst keeps an [online notebook](https://anotherdayinthedome.substack.com/p/on-writing-and-worlding-part-1-of) she only writes in while she is in motion. ##### **8. GIFTS** One of the best surprises you can make is a gift for someone else. Gifts allow you to direct your full attention to a specific person (or singular group of people) with something of yours at some imprecise time in the future. Sometimes gifts can be immaterial, made only to [honor](https://anotherdayinthedome.substack.com/p/on-eggs-part-3-secret?utm_source=profile&utm_medium=reader2#:~:text=%E2%80%9CI%20only%20make,do%20this%20well.) the recipient. Other times, they are simply about the act of creating the gift, merging recipient and sender. Regardless, they offer a new path of traversing the internet, following a path of love and close, dedicated attention. - Compile a [care package](https://garden.vincentli.space/making-a-place-on-the-web---garden) of the things you’ve found each month for close friends. - [Gift a website](https://you-are-laurel-right.neocities.org/) to your friend. - Facilitate the exchange of a [song](https://sentyouasong.com/) or make a [mixtape](https://shea.glitch.me/) to memorialize an event. - Make a [domain gift guide](https://chias.blog/2022/chias-2022-domain-gift-guide/). - Create a shared note to begin a letter exchange with a friend. Write something in it whenever you think of them. ##### **9. PERSONAL TRACES** As you travel through the Internet, what traces do you leave behind? What is your [tag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tag_(graffiti)) or stamp? How do your fellow travelers discover if this is a site you visit? In physical space, we can see and feel each other. Demonstrations are effective because we can stand shoulder-to-shoulder and occupy space, coming together to form a more powerful being. We can paste a poster, throw a tag, wear a statement t-shirt, hang a missing cat note, or interfere with the space in other ways. On the Internet, we might be able to make a user profile, allowing us to post and create a stream of likes and emoji reactions, but what do we do online when we are nothing but another IP address on a site made to load equally fast regardless of how many visitors? - Write your own [sign-off](https://sander.are.na/meg-miller/good-sign-offs), create your stamp, and imagine other identifying traces to leave across the sites you visit, like an emoji, a color, or a font. - Be on the lookout for guestbooks. You’ll [find](https://guestbook.goodenough.us/) them along the way, but if you are impatient, you can [search for them](https://wiby.me/?q=Guestbook). - Push yourself to leave a comment in open comment sections, especially on pieces of content that are hard to find or have not gone viral. - Play with [playhtml](https://playhtml.fun/), a collection of live games that persist your actions. - Install [World Wide Walls](https://chrome.google.com/webstore/detail/world-wide-walls/afidhlpnbjpnpilhjkglceebkakhemfb?hl=en-GB) to graffiti the internet. - Keep an eye out for places that preserve your actions: on [we-b.site](https://we-b.site/), leave a letter about your internet dreams and see who leaves behind fingerprints on the letterhead, and on [Mark Beasley’s website](https://mark-beasley.com/), watch the fireflies of cursors past flutter in the background. ##### **THE INTERNET OF YOU, ME, AND ALL OF US** The Internet is a vast space, laden with possibility. The indexed web[3](https://syllabusproject.org/syllabus-for-taking-an-internet-walk/#7ce73a4a-4d4f-4256-9d6c-0490804fddf8) alone has over 5 billion pages as of October 30, 2023, with countless more millions left unseen by the machine crawlers. In the early days of the internet, one of the first search engines, [Yahoo!, hired “surfers,”](https://www.nytimes.com/2016/07/17/technology/when-yahoo-ruled-the-valley-stories-of-the-original-surfers.html) people with particularly niche interests, to record and catalog new websites by hand. In those days, each site was crafted by hand by a person. Each site had a face you could see, and if desired, email. Now, these sites are hidden from our everyday experiences because they are invisible to our internet navigators. Instead, our defaults are hyper-SEOified links where there is no clear person behind the content. When we encounter the kind of content created for a computer-first internet, alarm bells should sound in our heads. Instead of accepting the default, remind yourself that you have an instinct for what draws you, hunt for handmade sites made with care, and return to the places and people you love. The internet is so much more than the loud and narrow portion we encounter daily. If we attend closely to the environment, we’ll start to see the life forces of everyday people, their dreams, frustrations, prayers, anxieties, and joys given willingly and freely. They deserve to be given the space and honor of being discovered. They are waiting for you to discover them. There is not one internet. There are [many](https://pluriverse.world/). The [fun](https://projects.kwon.nyc/internet-is-fun/), [poetic](https://www.are.na/chia/poetic-web), [homecooked](https://www.robinsloan.com/lab/specifying-spring-83/) internets are waiting for us. They are ours to [honor](https://we-b.site/), [personalize](https://archive.ph/2013.12.27-041357/http://frankchimero.com/blog/2013/12/homesteading-2014/), [queer](https://mirror.xyz/austinwadesmith.eth/wrBCeIWNsXbseQiLBj5jR_bkMFZ03nNYs4rg0lU8X2s), [mold](https://cristobal.space/writing/folk), [publish](https://publishsomethingonline.com/), [gather around](https://html.energy/), [world](https://handmade-web.net/exercises/homepage.html), and [maintain](https://queensmuseum.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/04/Ukeles-Manifesto-for-Maintenance-Art-1969.pdf), one [handmade website](http://luckysoap.com/statements/handmadeweb.html) at a time. On our terms. With each other. Slow and attentive. Will you join us on this walk? If new suggestions come to mind from your internet walking, we invite you to [add suggestions](https://coda.io/form/Walking-on-the-Internet-Syllabus-Community-Submission_dohHIi5PgN1) for future visitors, and [view the submission archive](https://coda.io/embed/v7sbtWRYi_/_sum-T?viewMode=embedplay). 1. Two places to start are Jane Jacobs’ *The Death and Life of Great American Cities* and Ivan Illich’s *Tools for Conviviality*. Both dive into how the building of cities became optimized for cars rather than people, and the desire consequences that ensued. [↩︎](https://syllabusproject.org/syllabus-for-taking-an-internet-walk/#897a0ef4-041d-4868-a860-1ee739262163-link) 2. Unfortunately, this is only for iPhone users, but if any Android users know of similar solutions, please contact us and we’d love to edit this to include them! [↩︎](https://syllabusproject.org/syllabus-for-taking-an-internet-walk/#a7199412-f87a-40fe-ac70-313cf45ecc27-link) 3. The websites that Google and other prominent search engines can see. Many sites are “invisible” under this definition, if they haven’t optimized their site for search engine discovery (the practice of SEO) which involves making the site more friendly to algorithmic reading rather than human visiting. This is more true for handmade, personal sites than it is for business sites that often hijack this optimization so that they can rank highly in search engines. [↩︎](https://syllabusproject.org/syllabus-for-taking-an-internet-walk/#7ce73a4a-4d4f-4256-9d6c-0490804fddf8-link)
